title: Influence and Change
author: Ian Hallett
summary: In the fifth and final part of his Leadership Operating System series, Ian Hallett takes up the domain where formal authority runs out: getting people you cannot instruct to commit to a direction and to change how they work. He opens with Paul O'Neill's twelve years at Alcoa, where a simple safety purpose and structural change cut lost-workday incidents from 1.86 to 0.2 per 100 workers. He draws on Yukl and Tracey's study of 128 managers, which found rational persuasion, inspiration and consultation produce commitment while pressure and appeals to authority do not, and on Herold's finding that good change practice helps even when a leader is not inspiring. His central tool is three conversations to hold before any announcement: the picture, the objector and the routine. He lays out seventeen behaviours across vision, influence and change, names four common failures (launch and leave, the pressure play, the slogan, the surprise), and closes with a one-week exercise.
points: A change has not happened until a specific weekly routine, report or rule is different, so name the routine that changes before you announce anything.
Take the proposal first to the person most likely to oppose it and ask what is wrong with it, because resistance found a week early is information rather than obstruction.
How you ask matters: rational persuasion, inspiration and consultation earn commitment, while pressure and appeals to authority earn only compliance.
A vision passes its test when someone two levels down can repeat it and say what it means for their own work.
The long middle of a change needs as many milestones and progress reports as the launch, or the team concludes it has been dropped.
quotes: When Gary Yukl and Bruce Tracey studied 128 managers, rated by 526 of their subordinates, 543 peers and 128 bosses, they looked at which ways of asking produced real commitment to a task. Rational persuasion, inspirational appeals and consultation came out best. Pressure, building a coalition and appealing to your authority came out worst.

David Herold and his colleagues looked specifically at change. They studied how leaders’ behaviour related to employees’ commitment to a change, and found that a leader’s vision and inspiration mattered more than change-management technique, most of all when the change hit people personally. But where people did not see their leader as inspiring, good change-management practice still raised their commitment.

This is the domain where authority runs out. As you move up, more of what you need sits with peers, senior people and other teams, none of whom report to you. The habits that worked with your own team, deciding and telling, start to cost you.
A change has not happened until the weekly routine is different.

Take the proposal to the person most likely to oppose it, before anyone else, and ask what is wrong with it. Change what should change. Whether or not they come round, they will have been heard first.
A direction people cannot repeat is a direction they cannot act on. The test of a vision is whether someone two levels down can say it back, and say what it means for their own work.
If you cannot name the routine that changes, you have an announcement and no change.
Resistance you discover in the meeting is obstruction; the same resistance discovered a week earlier is information.
